blocks.text: The standard hydrogen electrode is one of several types of half-cell that can be used as a reference electrode (Figure 10.4). It consists of hydrogen gas at 101 kPa pressure in equilibrium with H+ ions of concentration 1.00 mol dm-3, and a platinum electrode covered with platinum black in contact with the hydrogen gas and the H+ ions. Platinum black is finely divided platinum, which allows close contact of hydrogen gas and H+ ions so that the equilibrium between H2 gas and H+ ions is established quickly; the platinum electrode is inert and does not take part in the reaction. Standard electrode potential values for all half-cells are measured relative to this electrode: when it is connected to another half-cell, the voltmeter reading gives the standard electrode potential of that half-cell.

blocks.alt: Standard hydrogen electrode. A glass tube with a side inlet labelled Hydrogen gas supply at 1 atm pressure stands in a beaker of solution labelled H+ (1 mol/dm3). A platinum wire runs down the tube to a black platinum electrode. The tube widens at the bottom into a glass 'bell' with a hole in for H2 to bubble out; bubbles rise beside it.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 10.4 gives the acid concentration as '1mol/dm+3'; it is 1 mol/dm3 (1.00 mol dm-3), as drawn above.

The half-equation for the hydrogen electrode is 2H+(aq) + 2e- giving H2(g), E standard = 0.00 V, or equally H+(aq) + e- giving 1/2 H2(g), E standard = 0.00 V. The way the half-equation is balanced makes no difference to E standard, because the equation does not affect the tendency of the element to gain electrons; its voltage is arbitrarily fixed at 0.00 V.
